In their manuscript, “Machine learning-predicted insulin resistance is a risk factor for 12 site-
specific cancers” Lee et al use a previously described machine learning predicted insulin
sensitivity score to examine the impact of insulin resistance upon cancer incidence, arguing
that this score could have clinical utility for identifying patients who may benefit from
increased screening. The question the authors are asking is very significant to the field
because, as they highlight, it has been difficult to assess the impact of many of the
individual features of systemic metabolism upon cancer risk. Unfortunately, the findings
as presented need to be contextualized and interpreted in the context of both the obesity and
cancer literature as well as the cancer metabolism/genetics literature, for as written the authors
overstate the potential utility of this approach for cancer risk assessment and make claims
related to potential causal relationships (e.g. sun exposure in the obese) for which no
supportive data is provided, when activation of INSULIN signaling in certain mutational
contexts drive senescent phenotypes (as a potential example in melanoma). By contrast a
discussion of the mutational profiles of Uterine and Esophegeal tumors both of which
frequently mutate downstream components of the insulin signaling cascade (e.g. PI3K,
PTEN) may help to explain why these observations are biologically significant. The key issue
is that as described throughout their manuscript, the model relies heavily on BMI which is
already a known risk factor for 13 tumor types (Lauby-Secretan B, 2016 NEJM,
PMID:27557308). This well established observation diminishes the potential utility of the
model since BMI is one of its key inputs. It might be helpful to compare how BMI alone
performs as a risk factor for these tumor types, and then potentially examine the impact of
insulin sensitivity scores in patients with “normal” BMIs, as that population would not already
be identifiable by their physicians as being at elevated risk.
The work has significant promise, but as written it again needs to be contextualized in order
for readers to be able to understand its significance, which appears to be reduced from the
claims being made by the authors. In many ways as currently written this feels like a first step,
where they have applied their previously developed tool to a second data set, confirming its

Did you consider co-linearity between the various measures investigated, given that all these
variables are included in the AI-IR model?
Response
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In traditional regression models, co-
linearity between predictors can bias coefficient estimates and inflate standard errors, which
is a major concern. However, in machine learning models like XGboost (which we used for
AI-IR), the algorithm can naturally handle correlations among input features by modeling non-
linear interactions and making splits based on feature importance rather than relying on a
single coefficient per variable. Therefore, correlations among input parameters do not affect
the predictive performance of AI-IR.

lines 200 - 217: I'm not convinced this section adds to the paper, it feels like analysis for
analysis sake, rather than truly trying to understand the aetiology (which would be best done
individually for each cancer site)
Response
We thank the reviewer for this comment. Related to the previous point, in response to
reviewer #6 in the previous round, we defined “composite cancers” to increase
generalizability of our findings. We believe this composite approach adds value in two
important ways: (1) it increases statistical power by pooling less-common cancers, thereby
reducing the risk of false negatives; and (2) it provides a more clinically relevant and
generalizable picture of the overall cancer burden associated with AI-IR, which would be
overlooked if we only examined site-specific outcomes. While detailed investigation of
individual cancer sites is certainly important for understanding aetiology, the composite
cancer analysis serves a different purpose—offering a broader assessment of overall cancer
risk associated with AI-IR.
